quote: Yes, she will do for him very well. She will make him a very suitable wife.
why: 'Him' is Mr. Darcy, who has not been mentioned for many pages; the only men in the scene are Mr. Collins and Sir William, so a reader or listener can easily take the joke to be about the wrong man.
suggestion: Yes, she will do for Mr. Darcy very well. She will make him a very suitable wife.

quote: Elizabeth suspected she was the first person who had ever dared to trifle with such grand impertinence.
why: 'Such grand impertinence' reads as if Elizabeth is the impertinent one; the point is that Lady Catherine's own lofty rudeness has never been teased before.
suggestion: Elizabeth suspected she was the first person who had ever dared to make light of such lofty rudeness.

quote: Lady Catherine, Sir William, and Mr. and Mrs. Collins sat down to quadrille. Since Miss de Bourgh chose to play casino,
why: Quadrille and casino are period card games; 'play casino' in particular now suggests gambling at a casino.
suggestion: sat down to quadrille, a card game for four. Since Miss de Bourgh chose to play the card game casino,

quote: Until Elizabeth remembered that there might be that the family might have other church posts to hand out, she could not understand the sacrifice of so many hours.
why: Duplicated, broken clause ('there might be that the family might have'); also 'the family' is unclear. It should be Lady Catherine who has church posts to give.
suggestion: Until Elizabeth remembered that Lady Catherine might have other church posts to give away, she could not understand the sacrifice of so many hours.

quote: His arrival was soon known at the parsonage, for Mr. Collins spent the whole morning walking within sight of the gates opening onto Hunsford Lane, in order to have
why: The paragraph breaks off mid-sentence and continues in 30.7 ('the earliest confirmation of it.'). A reader sees a truncated sentence, and in audio it will be split across two segments. Merge 30.6 and 30.7 (alignment permitting) or move the break to a sentence boundary.
suggestion: His arrival was soon known at the parsonage, for Mr. Collins spent the whole morning walking within sight of the gates opening onto Hunsford Lane, in order to have the earliest confirmation of it.

quote: There were two nephews of Lady Catherine requiring them,
why: 'Them' refers back to 'his respects' in the previous sentence, which is too far away and too abstract; the clause reads as if the nephews need something.
suggestion: There were two nephews of Lady Catherine to whom he owed his respects,

quote: And though there were not many of her acquaintances she did not prefer to him,
why: Stacked negatives ('not many ... she did not prefer') make readers stop to work out that she dislikes him.
suggestion: And though she preferred almost any of her acquaintances to him,

quote: _His_ eyes had been quickly and repeatedly turned toward them with a look of curiosity, and that her Ladyship eventually shared the feeling was more openly shown, for she did not hesitate to call out:
why: A 'that'-clause as subject ('that her Ladyship ... shared the feeling was more openly shown') has to be re-read.
suggestion: _His_ eyes had quickly and repeatedly turned toward them with a look of curiosity, and her Ladyship soon showed the same curiosity more openly, for she did not hesitate to call out:

quote: by coming over in such state to listen
why: 'In such state' (meaning with such ceremony or grandeur) is no longer understood and may read as 'in such a state' (agitated).
suggestion: by coming over so grandly to listen

quote: that he might just as easily have married _her_, had she been his relative.
why: The sentence mentions Miss de Bourgh just before, so '_her_' seems to mean Miss de Bourgh; it actually means Miss Bingley. That reverses the joke.
suggestion: that he might just as well have married Miss Bingley, had she been his relative.

quote: Colonel Fitzwilliam had made it clear that he had no intentions at all,
why: 'No intentions at all' is too bare now; it means he has no intention of courting or marrying her.
suggestion: Colonel Fitzwilliam had made it clear that he had no intention of courting her,

quote: His sense of her inferiority, of it being beneath him,
why: 'It' has no antecedent (it means the match, or marrying her).
suggestion: His sense of her inferiority, of such a match being beneath him,

quote: But the approaching figure was now close enough to see her, and stepping forward eagerly, called her name.
why: The second clause has no subject. As written, 'the approaching figure' does the calling, which is awkward, and the 'and' clause is missing 'he'.
suggestion: But he was now close enough to see her, and, stepping forward eagerly, he called her name.

quote: who had chances to observe him in unguarded moments that Mr. Darcy never had.
why: Darcy is the letter-writer, so 'Mr. Darcy' here reads as Darcy referring to himself in the third person. It actually means his father.
suggestion: who had chances to observe him in unguarded moments that my father never had.

quote: Two offenses of a very different nature, and by no means equal in seriousness, you charged me with last night.
why: Structural point: the whole of Darcy's long letter (Bingley, family, Wickham, Georgiana) is one paragraph of about 2,000 words. Individual sentences are clear, but in the reader and in paragraph-level audio it is a wall of text with no resting points. Split at topic boundaries if the aligned original allows it (e.g. before 'My own part must now be explained', 'Regarding that other, more serious accusation', 'My excellent father died', 'I must now mention something').

quote: Of his previous way of life, nothing had been known in Hertfordshire except what he'd told
why: The paragraph breaks mid-sentence; 36.4 begins 'them himself.' Same split-sentence defect as 30.6/30.7.
suggestion: Of his previous way of life, nothing had been known in Hertfordshire except what he'd told them himself.

quote: make up for those minor failings she would try to classify Mr. Darcy's description of years of idleness and vice as being
why: Tangled clause ending in a stranded 'as being'. Readers have to reverse-engineer it.
suggestion: make up for what she would try to count as minor failings, which was how she hoped to classify the years of idleness and vice Mr. Darcy described

quote: she had to admit that Mr. Bingley, when questioned by Jane, had long ago confirmed his blamelessness in the affair—that, proud and off-putting as his manners were,
why: One very long chain of 'that ...' clauses joined by dashes, with 'his' switching between Bingley and Darcy. A listener loses the thread; 'his blamelessness' seems to mean Bingley's.
suggestion: she had to admit that Mr. Bingley, when questioned by Jane, had long ago confirmed Mr. Darcy's blamelessness in the affair. She also had to admit that, proud and off-putting as Darcy's manners were,

quote: But whatever they might be, it's easy to imagine how eagerly she read through them,
why: In chapter 36 the narration suddenly uses contractions ('it's', 'didn't', 'wouldn't', 'she'd', 'couldn't', 'hadn't') throughout, where chapters 25–35 keep narration uncontracted. The shift in register is noticeable. Contractions in dialogue are fine.
suggestion: But whatever they might be, it is easy to imagine how eagerly she read through them,

quote: satisfied my vanity with useless or pointless suspicion
why: 'Useless or pointless' is redundant and flat, which weakens the climax of the self-reproach.
suggestion: satisfied my vanity with idle and unworthy suspicion
